title: Private CCTV Cannot Be Aimed to Invade a Neighbour's Privacy: Allahabad HC
meta_description: Allahabad HC holds a private CCTV camera cannot interfere with a neighbour's privacy, leaving removal disputes to the District Magistrate.
bench: Justice Ajit Kumar and Justice Garima Prashad
case_name: Yogendra Maurya v. State of U.P. and Others
body: Two neighbours arguing over where a CCTV camera points is not the kind of dispute that usually reaches a High Court, but that is what brought Yogendra Maurya to Allahabad. His complaint was that a camera installed by the family living next door had been angled in a way that captured the entry and exit points of his own house, so that anyone visiting him or leaving his home ended up on his neighbour's recording. He asked the court to intervene. On 26 October 2026, a bench of Justice Ajit Kumar and Justice Garima Prashad gave him part of what he wanted, though not in the form he had asked for it.

The bench did not get into whether the particular camera in Maurya's case actually crossed the line. What it did was lay down the principle that should decide that question when it does come up: a private CCTV camera cannot be installed or positioned in a manner that interferes with a neighbour's privacy. That is a straightforward enough statement, but it fills a gap that has become more pressing as home security cameras have gone from rare to routine in Indian residential colonies, often bought and installed without anyone thinking through where the lens actually ends up pointing.

What the court did not do is order the camera taken down or moved. Instead, it left the fact-finding to someone closer to the ground. If Maurya wants the camera's position examined and possibly changed, he has to file an application for its removal, and the District Magistrate has been directed to consider and decide that application within one month of it being filed. The High Court set the rule; the District Magistrate has to apply it to this particular camera, this particular wall, this particular angle.

That division of labour is deliberate rather than a dodge. A writ court is poorly placed to inspect a camera's field of view, measure angles, or weigh one neighbour's security concerns against another's privacy on the facts of a single installation, especially when the dispute could just as easily turn on something a site visit would reveal and an affidavit would not. Routing that inquiry to the District Magistrate, who has the administrative machinery to send someone out to look, keeps the High Court's ruling at the level of principle while giving Maurya an actual, time-bound route to a decision on his specific complaint.

A month is a short window for a local authority to receive an application, assess a disputed camera installation, and issue a decision, and that tight clock says something about how the court expects this kind of complaint to be handled. Two neighbours are not meant to go on living indefinitely with one of them aggrieved by a camera the other refuses to adjust, each waiting out the other in the hope the friction simply fades. Anyone in Maurya's position elsewhere in Uttar Pradesh facing a similarly placed camera now has a template to follow: approach the District Magistrate directly, armed with this ruling, rather than filing a fresh writ petition and waiting months for a High Court to weigh in on facts a district officer can just as easily establish by visiting the spot.

Housing societies and residents' welfare associations, which often end up mediating exactly this kind of friction between adjoining plot owners, now have a legal standard to point to rather than negotiating purely on goodwill. A society that has so far handled camera complaints informally, by telling a resident to simply ask the neighbour to adjust the angle, can instead point an uncooperative owner toward the District Magistrate's jurisdiction under this ruling, backed by a fixed one-month timeline rather than a request that carries no consequence if ignored.

For housing societies, builders of independent houses, and anyone installing a home security system in a street with close-set plots, the ruling is a reminder that a camera's lawful purpose does not stretch to cover whatever its lens happens to pick up. Protecting one's own doorstep is a legitimate reason to install a camera; sweeping a neighbour's gate, porch or visitors into the same frame is not something that purpose automatically justifies, and a complaint about it now has a clear forum and a fixed clock rather than an open-ended grievance with nowhere obvious to go.
why_it_matters: Home CCTV cameras have become common in Indian residential areas with little attention paid to where they actually point, and disputes between neighbours over camera placement have had no clear forum to go to. This ruling gives such disputes a defined route, a time-bound application to the District Magistrate, rather than leaving an aggrieved neighbour to either tolerate the intrusion or pursue a writ petition. Anyone installing or objecting to a home security camera in Uttar Pradesh now has a concrete standard and process to point to.
card_summary: Allahabad High Court rules a private CCTV camera cannot be positioned to intrude on a neighbour's privacy, and directs any removal application to the District Magistrate for decision within a month.
card_tip: A neighbour objecting to a wrongly angled CCTV camera can apply directly to the District Magistrate for a decision within one month, rather than filing a fresh writ petition.
verification_notes: The case name, writ petition number (Writ C No. 42270 of 2026), the bench (Justice Ajit Kumar and Justice Garima Prashad), the core allegation (camera exposing entry and exit points of the petitioner's house), the holding that private CCTV cannot interfere with a neighbour's privacy, and the direction to the District Magistrate to decide any removal application within one month are confirmed across Bar and Bench, LiveLaw and Law Chakra. The order date of 26 October 2026 is as reported by Law Chakra; Bar and Bench's own report is dated 3 November 2026, which this draft treats as the publication date rather than the decision date, consistent with the rule to use the decision date. Counsel names reported by only one source are not included here.
